rewrites.summary:
Guatemala demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: Asociación Lambda's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022 — hundreds of incidents and dozens of deaths — with 35 victims saying they intended to flee the country. Guatemalan officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds they are not “biological women.” There is no legal gender recognition and no SOGI hate-crime statute (a 2022 law actually increased penalties for “aggravated” LGBT visibility before being struck down).

Congress has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives (Law 5276, the 2022 “Life and Family Protection” bill, later shelved after protests). The community is organised (a local group such as Lambda, plus trans collectives) but under pressure. Tourist areas (Antigua, Atitlán) are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from the general violence level.

The consequence axis if a trans visitor is arrested is documented and dangerous: Human Rights Watch (7 October 2020) records that Guatemalan authorities facilitate anti-trans violence by placing trans women in men's prisons, exposing them to violence including sexual assault — activist Bárbara Herrarte (Redmmutrans) described her time in a men's prison: 'Always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him.' Placement operated by birth sex in the men's prison system as of 2020, with no gender-identity-based placement policy, no special trans unit, and no trans-specific solitary/segregation practice on record; in a country with no legal gender recognition, a detained trans visitor faces men's-prison placement with documented sexual-assault risk and no documented custody rule or court ruling anchoring a remedy.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Regional legal framework: a 2017 advisory opinion of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advanced gender recognition in four regional countries, including this one, with compliance still uncertain; a vociferous opposition movement defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash in all four.

Legislative flux: early-2022 bills sought to erase gender-identity protections and restrict legal recognition, and anti-trans initiatives have repeatedly advanced in the national legislature.

The custody finding sits inside a regional and asylum frame: the Human Rights Watch report documenting birth-sex prison placement is the Guatemala chapter of a three-country report covering Guatemala, El Salvador and Honduras that also examines obstacles to asylum in the United States; it documents no trans-specific custody policy or court ruling for Guatemala, and the same report records that the LGBTQ organisation Lambda flags forced internal displacement from violence generally — refugee/context material, not a visitor-facing protection.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The femicide-law exclusion of trans women and the absence of legal gender recognition are resident-facing; the documented violence toll — 147 recorded cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders in 2022 (hundreds of incidents, dozens of deaths) — falls on residents.

The organised community (a local group and trans collectives) operates under pressure from the repeated legislative attacks.

Resident custody: the documented practice of placing trans women in men's prisons by birth sex, with sexual-assault exposure (activist Bárbara Herrarte's account), governs residents held in the system, and Lambda flags forced internal displacement of LGBTI people from violence generally — a resident burden; a visitor meets the custody practice only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: how the general violence level in communities outside the tourist areas applies to visitors is unquantified — general gang violence affects all travellers, and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from it.

Unverified: no documented trans-visitor incidents appear in the current sources, and the femicide-law exclusion is resident-facing though it signals institutional stance.

Prison axis: the birth-sex placement finding rests on a single Human Rights Watch documentation (7 October 2020); no Guatemalan law, regulation, court ruling or custody policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented — in a country without legal gender recognition, that absence cannot be read as a protected standard.
rewrites.notes: rt005 VIS: folded verified prison-axis source (HRW 2020: birth-sex men's-prison placement with sexual-assault exposure; no gender-identity placement policy, special trans unit or trans-specific solitary/segregation practice; no custody policy or court ruling documented) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
South Korea is broadly workable for trans visitors — there is no criminalisation, courts have protected trans people's restroom access and ruled favourably on legal gender recognition, and Seoul hosts one of Asia's largest Pride parades. There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner, and no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering services. No severe incidents involving trans visitors are documented. Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are welcoming; outside them, more caution is warranted.

The consequence axis of an arrest is largely undocumented: no source in this record describes how transgender prisoners are housed in South Korea's civilian prison system — no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no special unit, and no solitary/segregation practice — and no civilian trans-prisoner case surfaced. The one documented trans-in-state-placement case is military rather than civilian: Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, a transgender conscript, was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical/mental handicap; she died by suicide in March 2021; the Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021; and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty — a harsh institutional default corrected by the courts only after death. For a detained trans visitor, civilian-prison placement is simply unknown: in a legal system where legal gender recognition is possible and courts have repeatedly ruled for trans people, recourse would likely exist, but the placement practice itself is unverified — not a verified midpoint and not verified safe.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Compared with its closest comparable peers, the legal baseline has documented gaps: no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and no same-sex marriage. Policy and litigation flux: a December 2024 martial-law crisis and related assembly-freedom questions, a 2024 constitutional ruling recognising same-sex partners' healthcare rights, and organised conservative opposition set a moving political backdrop rather than direct street-level risk.

Custody-axis framing: the only trans-in-state-placement case on record is a military conscript case — Byun Hui-su's discharge, death, posthumous reinstatement and line-of-duty recognition — rather than a civilian prison case; the criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel (Military Criminal Act article 92-6, up to two years' imprisonment) and the exclusion of transgender people from military service are resident-conscript-facing, not visitor-facing.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The court-based LGR process (surgery was historically required but courts are moving to allow changes without it), the hospital-ward 'transgender blind spot' (the health ministry cannot answer how to accommodate trans patients), school-bathroom friction, and the military-service harassment data (12% of trans people assigned male at birth who served in the mandatory military experienced sexual harassment or violence — this affects Korean conscripts, not foreign visitors) are all resident-facing.

Further resident data: 67% of trans youth report hearing transphobic remarks from teachers; same-sex conduct is criminalised in the military under the military criminal code (upheld in 2023); and a nationwide survey documents a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care.

The one documented institutional case is a conscript's: Byun Hui-su stood under mandatory military service and the military criminal code — legal machinery that does not reach visitors; transgender people are excluded from military service, and the military same-sex-conduct ban governs serving personnel, while nothing is documented about how trans people are housed in the civilian prison system at all.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Foreign-tourist taxi scams and shopping complaints rose 71% in 2024 — general, not trans-specific.

One source — a supreme-court family-register decision — could not be retrieved at research time, so that ruling's detail rests on its summary. No border-screening or document-handling practice specific to trans visitors is documented in this record.

Prison axis: no South Korean rule, regulation, case or practice is documented on civilian trans-prisoner housing — no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no special unit, no solitary/segregation practice; the only state-placement case on record is the military discharge case (an administrative discharge, not a prison-housing case). Where a detained trans visitor would be housed in the civilian system is unverified, and that gap cannot be read as evidence of either identity-based placement or mistreatment.
rewrites.notes: rt005 VIS: folded verified prison-axis source (Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in South Korea': Byun Hui-su military discharge/death/posthumous reinstatement; no civilian trans-prisoner placement rule, special unit or solitary/segregation practice documented) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Mexico pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Twenty-two of its 32 states offer administrative legal gender recognition, Mexico City and Nayarit have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist. Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — the second-highest figure in the Americas after Brazil — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated by region.

In major tourist destinations and central Mexico City, heavily policed and progressively governed, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is Mexico's general crime environment. Use the Admin Divisions view: state-level scores range from among Latin America's best (Mexico City) to levels comparable with its most dangerous regions.

The consequence axis if a trans visitor is arrested is undocumented: the only prison-axis finding in this record — a Wikipedia survey of LGBTQ people in prison — contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement in Mexico (no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no trans special units, no solitary/segregation practice); its sole Mexico-specific item is a July 2007 Mexico City policy, adopted through the human-rights commission (CDHDF), allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation. In a federation where legal gender recognition is state-by-state and official discrimination and near-total impunity for anti-trans violence are documented, where a detained trans visitor would be housed is unverifiable and cannot be assumed to follow identity.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Marriage equality nationwide — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.

Custody-policy context: the sole Mexico-specific prison finding in this record — Mexico City's July 2007 same-sex conjugal-visit policy stemming from a 2003 anti-discrimination law, applying to all Mexico City prisons, with visitors not required to be married to the inmate — is a city-level custody-conditions measure, not a placement rule; it shows local recognition of sexual-orientation rights inside one city's prisons without any documented counterpart for trans-prisoner placement anywhere in the country.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The state-by-state administrative LGR regime and the transfemicide statutes (Mexico City, Nayarit) are resident-facing; the 71-murder toll falls overwhelmingly on local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit.

Resident custody: the documented prison-axis finding — the 2007 Mexico City same-sex conjugal-visit policy applying to all Mexico City prisons — governs inmates, and the undocumented trans-prisoner placement practice (no birth-sex vs identity rule, no trans special units, no solitary/segregation data in any source in this record) concerns residents held in the system; a visitor meets either only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Cartel violence, kidnapping, and theft drive several governments to advise caution or non-essential travel avoidance for parts of Mexico — a risk independent of any personal characteristic.

Prison axis: the single prison-axis source is thin for Mexico — it documents no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no trans special units and no solitary/segregation practice, and its only Mexico-specific item (the 2007 Mexico City conjugal-visit policy) says nothing about where trans prisoners are housed; whether a detained trans visitor would be held federally or by a state, and how documents would interact with placement, are unverified in these sources.
rewrites.notes: rt005 VIS: folded verified prison-axis source (Wikipedia 'LGBTQ people in prison', Mexico section: thin — 2007 Mexico City same-sex conjugal-visit policy only; no trans placement rule, special unit or solitary/segregation practice documented) into visible fields as thin-data consequence evidence per LANE_SPECS rule 8b; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Greece is a workable destination with a clear law-versus-practice gap. The legal framework is among Europe's strongest — it ranks 7th on the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map, has banned conversion therapy and intersex infant surgery, has a hate-crime law covering gender identity, and legalised same-sex marriage in 2024 (the first Orthodox-majority country to do so). There are no trans-specific border or bathroom restrictions, and the government is progressive with an improving trajectory.

But the social reality lags the law. A mob of about 150 people assaulted two trans people in Thessaloniki; an European Court of Human Rights case documented police detention and mistreatment of trans sex workers; surveys show Greeks are markedly more avoidant of public LGBTI visibility than the EU average (63% avoid holding hands); and the UK Foreign Office has issued an LGBTQ travel warning for Greece. Major tourist destinations — Mykonos, Athens's Gazi district, Thessaloniki — are welcoming; outside them the climate is rougher than the law suggests.

The consequence axis of an arrest is a documented default-plus-petition system: placement of trans women detainees started from the registered sex — the four trans women transferred to Korydallou's women's prisons on 4 December 2021 had previously been held at Trikala and Corfu prisons, effectively isolated and treated inconsistently with their self-identified gender — and a decision of that date by the General Secretary for Crime-Prevention Policy created an on-request transfer route to women's facilities, the first documented transfers of trans prisoners to a women's facility in the country. No special trans units and no rule covering trans men's placement are documented. A detained trans visitor therefore meets a registered-sex default with an on-request transfer route that demonstrably exists but runs through administrative petition — a workable-but-request-dependent outcome consistent with the country's law-versus-practice gap.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Same-sex marriage legal since 2024 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners; the UK Foreign Office LGBTQ travel warning is a general queer-traveler signal.

Custody-policy context: the 4 December 2021 transfer route was an administrative decision of the General Secretary for Crime-Prevention Policy (the transfers of the four women — three Greek, one Bulgarian — followed each woman's petition), not legislation; the Wikipedia overview of Greek LGBTQ rights confirms under 'Correctional Facilities' that placement starts from the registered sex, with the on-request transfer route for trans women — correctional-administration machinery, not a visitor-facing protection.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Resident-facing climate data from the sources: the EU FRA LGBTIQ survey country sheet (2024) records Greek residents' avoidance and discrimination burden — 63% avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (EU average 53%), 36% avoid certain locations for fear of assault, only 35% are open about being LGBTIQ, and 28% felt discriminated at work; the mob assault on two trans people in Thessaloniki and the documented police stops and mistreatment of transgender sex workers in Athens (the ECtHR case) fell on residents.

The documented custody practice is resident-facing: the registered-sex placement default and the 4 December 2021 on-request transfer route govern prisoners held in the Greek system — the documented transferees were a Bulgarian and three Greek nationals held at Trikala and Corfu prisons; a visitor meets the practice only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific travel advisory beyond the UK Foreign Office's general LGBTQ note; ordinary tourist-season crime affects all travellers.

Prison axis: how the on-request transfer route operates in practice — processing time, success rates, conditions before a transfer, and its application to a foreign visitor detained while travelling — is not documented; no trans special units and no rule covering trans men's placement appear in any source, the four December 2021 transfers are the only documented case series, and the Wikipedia/LiFO sources agree that default placement had followed the male facilities until that decision.
rewrites.notes: rt005 VIS: folded 2 verified prison-axis sources (LiFO 2021: four trans detainees transferred to Korydallou women's prisons after petitioning; Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Greece' Correctional Facilities: registered-sex placement default with a 4 Dec 2021 on-request transfer route, no special units, no rule covering trans men) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Nigeria is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the SSMPA (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 northern states apply Sharia law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender TikToker known as "Abuja Area Mama" was found beaten and dead on a highway in Abuja; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one has been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" — the SSMPA has been described as a "weaponised" law — and dating-app "kito" gangs use Grindr to lure victims into assault and robbery. The UK Foreign Office has warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks.

A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is NOT explicitly criminalized nationally (the SSMPA targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. But the Sharia death penalty, the trans-specific killing with impunity, the police brutality, and the UK advisory make this an environment to avoid entirely.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented through the country's only recorded trans-imprisonment case: Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine, and served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked 'which prison they will keep the crossdresser in', and the article does not record whether she was assigned to a male or female section — placement was discretionary — while an October 2024 investigative panel found the maximum-security placement itself unlawful for a first-time offender under the Nigerian Correctional Service Act. For a trans visitor, the SSMPA's 14-year exposure already applies to tourists; on top of that, detention would land in a prison system with a documented discretionary, unlawfully-assigned placement practice and no recorded housing standard for trans prisoners.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
The SSMPA (14 years, applies to tourists) and the Sharia death penalty in 12 northern states are direct risks for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active; dating-app "kito" gangs are a direct app-user risk.

Custody-litigation context: the only trans-prisoner "ruling" on record is the October 2024 investigative panel finding that Bobrisky's maximum-security placement violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender; the same panel dismissed the bribery allegations that had prompted it — an administrative outcome in a celebrity case, not a rule fixing trans-prisoner housing anywhere in the country.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The documented violence and impunity fall on residents: the killing of the trans TikToker "Abuja Area Mama" with no arrests six months on, police beatings and bribe-extortion of people perceived as gay, the attacks and lost job prospects documented a decade into the SSMPA, and the law's documented reach beyond marriage — cohabitation, any public show of same-sex amorous relationship, and gay organisations criminalised with 10-14 years' prison, with police torture and arbitrary arrests under it (as documented in the 2016 human-rights report).

The recorded imprisonment case is a resident case: Bobrisky served her sentence in a Nigerian prison, and the discretionary placement practice (male or female section left unrecorded, the maximum-security assignment found unlawful for a first-time offender) governs residents held in the system — a visitor meets it only through arrest and detention, which the criminalisation of same-sex conduct makes a live prospect for trans visitors perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Terrorism (Boko Haram in the northeast), kidnapping, and violent crime affect all travellers in many regions; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Prison axis: no Nigerian law, regulation or policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented in any source in this record; the Bobrisky biography does not record which section she was assigned to, the October 2024 panel finding concerns the lawfulness of a placement rather than a housing standard, and the Reuters report on the proposed cross-dressing ban could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 401), so that bill's status rests on its written summary.
rewrites.notes: rt005 VIS: folded verified prison-axis source (Wikipedia 'Bobrisky': 2024 Kirikiri maximum-security imprisonment, open question of which section a crossdresser would be kept in, October 2024 panel finding the max-security placement unlawful for a first-time offender; no placement law, special unit or segregation practice documented) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.
